mock_note: All cell values except the development profiles (NO, UK) are placeholders generated by scripts/site/build_site_data.py. They illustrate the target product and are not findings.

features.name: CB_LINK_ONLINE
features.question: Can the issuing central bank / core-system operator, in the standard online mode, directly or through a routinely available link attribute a transaction to a person?
features.qualifiers: actor = CB or operator; scope = standard online mode
features.traps: "CB will not *use* the data" ≠ cannot link. Extraordinary re-identification → F9, not here. Pseudonymisation at the CB counts as *no* only if the CB holds no routine key to identity.

features.name: PSP_LINK_ONLINE
features.question: Can the user's payment service provider routinely attribute an online transaction to a person?
features.qualifiers: actor = PSP; scope; payer vs payee
features.traps: KYC at onboarding does **not** imply F2 = yes (§6). Bearer/token designs where the PSP sees no transaction record → no.

features.name: LAWFUL_ACCESS_ROUTE
features.question: Does the institution document a route by which a public authority can obtain person-attributable transaction data, and through whom?
features.values: via_PSP / via_CB / via_both / none_stated / n/d (+ named authority in `actor`, process in `modality`)
features.qualifiers: actor = which authority; modality = legal process named; legal_state when derived from law
features.traps: Descriptive only: no channel split, no aggregate, no outcome. "Same rules as for bank accounts" or "lawful basis under existing law" is a route via_PSP only if the PSP is named as the holder; otherwise n/d with the sentence quoted. Suspicion-based STRs are a route (via_PSP). Never coded ROUTINE/TARGETED: that distinction depends on law outside the corpus (v1 experience, NO and UK).

features.name: PRIVATE_OFFLINE_AVAILABLE
features.question: Is an offline mode an adopted commitment in which individual transfer details are not routinely transmitted to or linked with a person by the CB or PSP, including at later synchronisation?
features.traps: Offline offered but privacy undescribed → unknown. Tested capability ≠ adopted. An adopted decision *not* to offer offline → no.

features.name: INDEPENDENT_ACCESS_GATE
features.question: Does targeted public-authority access require prior authorisation by an independent body under an applicable adopted rule?

features.name: NO_COMMERCIAL_REUSE_WITHOUT_CONSENT
features.question: Is commercial use of PSP transaction data without separate user consent prohibited by an adopted rule?

features.name: LOW_ID_ROUTE
features.question: Is there an adopted retail mode in which an eligible user can hold/pay up to a stated limit without verified personal identity (including verification via another account)?
features.qualifiers: limits; onboarding; link to an identified account
features.traps: KYC-lite that still verifies identity ≠ no identity. Never labelled "anonymity".

features.name: ONBOARDING_ID
features.question: Does opening a standard wallet require verified personal identity?
features.traps: Descriptive only; **not** a premise for F2.

features.name: TARGETED_REIDENTIFICATION
features.question: Can an online transaction be attributed to a person afterwards under defined extraordinary conditions? By whom, under what condition?
features.traps: Prevents reading F1 = no as absolute. Descriptive only.

features.name: PROGRAMMABLE_RESTRICTIONS
features.question: Does the adopted design allow issuer/state-imposed restrictions on use (purpose, expiry, blocking) beyond AML?
features.traps: Must distinguish state-imposed restrictions from user-requested conditional payments. Lower priority; dropped if the pilot shows it overloads coders.

features.name: STATED_OBJECTIVES
features.question: Which objectives does the institution declare, and did it explicitly rank one as main?
features.values: `stated_objectives` = set of flags {payment_modernisation, financial_inclusion, monetary_sovereignty_transmission, cash_substitute_resilience, aml_cft_tax_enforcement, innovation_competitiveness}, each with a quote; `primary_status` = one_primary / several_joint / unranked / conflict / n/d; `primary_objectives` only when ranking is documented
features.traps: "CBDC will comply with AML rules" is a design requirement, not an objective. A zero flag means "not documented in the checked sources", not absence of motive. Word frequencies may go in an appendix as "linguistic emphasis"; they never set the flags.

features.name: LEDGER_TECHNOLOGY
features.question: Which ledger technology does the design use or has it chosen?
features.values: conventional_centralised / permissioned_DLT / permissionless_DLT / hybrid / undecided / n/d; `platform` free text (e.g. Hyperledger Besu, Corda, custom); `claim_status` decides whether the value is a test or a choice
features.qualifiers: claim_status; transaction_scope (online core vs offline component)
features.traps: Tested platforms in a PoC are `tested`, never adopted. "Technology-neutral" statements → undecided. Permissionless is expected to be empty among adopted designs (stated in advance). Descriptive, outside the type and Y; external criterion: comparable fields in the BIS (Auer–Cornelli–Frost) and Atlantic Council trackers are used for a concurrent-validity check of the extraction, never to set the value.

F1.quote: Norges Bank should not have information about individuals' CBDC holdings or payments.
F1.justification: The latest document lists, as a design feature, that the central bank should hold no identity information. Footnote 22 adds that it would have no 'information about the identity of individual CBDC account holders' (doc 6 p. 16). The same report says the list 'must be considered a rough draft' because introduction is 'currently not warranted' (doc 6 p. 16, p. 2), so the claim is an option, not an adopted commitment. Test case 1 also showed the central bank without access to personal data (doc 6 p. 11; doc 7 p. 8-11), but that is tested only. 'Should not have information' is weaker than 'cannot link', and pseudonymous addresses are visible on the ledger (doc 6 p. 12); the state is therefore partial, not documented.

F2.quote: Hvis alle kontrolloppgavene skal foretas av tredjeparter, må det teknisk være mulig for tredjeparter å følge transaksjoner på samme måte som med bankinnskudd i dag.
F2.justification: The 2021 report states that, if third parties carry out customer control, wallet providers must be able to follow transactions as with bank deposits today, including who a user receives from and pays to (doc 4 p. 23). The 2026 report confirms that KYC/AML would be done by banks or wallet providers, the same as for other payment services (doc 6 p. 16). In the sandbox, banks link customers to ledger addresses in their own registers (doc 7 p. 9-10). The statement is conditional and no design was adopted (doc 6 p. 2), so the value is an option and the state is partial. It is not an inference from KYC alone.

F3.quote: Dette omfatter blant annet identitetskontroll ved on-boarding av brukere, kontroll med transaksjoner og rapportering av mistenkelige transaksjoner.
F3.justification: Customer control, which explicitly includes suspicious-transaction reporting, is meant to be carried out by third parties (doc 4 p. 23). The 2026 report repeats that KYC/AML would be performed by banks or wallet providers (doc 6 p. 16). Under the contract, suspicion-based reports held by a named PSP are a via_PSP route. The receiving authority is not named, and responsibility for transaction monitoring under the AML Act is left unresolved (doc 5 p. 14-15), so the state is partial.

F4.quote: Kravet dreier seg om at systemet kan fungere uavhengig av bankenes betalingssystemer og også fungere for offline-betalinger i en periode.
F4.justification: Offline payment capability appears as a required characteristic (doc 4 p. 8, p. 21; doc 2 p. 17), but no adopted offline mode exists because introduction was rejected (doc 6 p. 2). No document describes privacy of offline transfers at synchronisation. Under the rule that offline without a privacy description is unknown, F4 is unknown. One passage suggests anonymous payments would be unavailable offline, which points against privacy but is also only an option.

F7.quote: For både hovedløsningen og den alternative løsningen kan det vurderes om det bør være mulighet for begrenset tilgang for personer som ikke tilfredsstiller kravene som nevnt over
F7.justification: A reduced-identification tier is only 'considered' (doc 2 p. 26). Anonymous prepaid cards are discussed as a possibility for the closed account solution (doc 4 p. 24). No mode is adopted. Because lower-identification routes are mentioned, the §6.6a inference of F7 = no does not apply, so the value stays unknown.

F8.quote: KYC and AML checks of CBDC users would have to be performed by banks or other market participants that offer wallets for CBDC storage and transactions to their customers.
F8.justification: The latest report requires KYC checks of CBDC users by wallet-providing banks. Earlier reports set access requirements equal to opening a Norwegian bank account (doc 2 p. 26). This amounts to verified identity at onboarding. It is a draft design feature for a CBDC that was not introduced (doc 6 p. 2, p. 16), so it is an option and the state is partial.

F9.quote: vil likevel innebære at det må gjøres koblinger mellom «tokens» og identitet, for eksempel ved on-boarding av nye brukere, store transaksjoner og mistenkelige transaksjoner.
F9.justification: Customer-control requirements imply linking tokens to identity for large and suspicious transactions, with identity data held in external registers (doc 4 p. 23-24). Keys allowing authorised actors to unlock information under procedures are also discussed (doc 4 p. 38). The 2026 test report notes that addresses could be linked to identity, e.g. via court orders (doc 6 p. 12). All of this is option or tested, not adopted.

F10.quote: CBDC should not be programmable money, and programmability, if implemented, should be at the payment service level.
F10.justification: The 2026 report rejects programmable money at the money level and keeps programmability at the payment-service level, which excludes issuer-imposed restrictions. The 2021 report had discussed purpose-bound social support only with caution (doc 4 p. 41). The latest position wins for that matter. It remains an option in a 'rough draft' list (doc 6 p. 16), so the state is partial.

F12.quote: The sandbox solution in this test case is based on Hyperledger Besu, which is a permissioned ledger compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
F12.justification: The tested platforms are permissioned DLTs: Besu (doc 7 p. 9) and Fabric (doc 7 p. 12). The 2026 report says a retail ledger 'should probably be based on blockchain technology' and a wholesale ledger 'private' (doc 6 p. 17, p. 19). That remains a draft and no CBDC was adopted (doc 6 p. 2), so the claim status is tested, not adopted. Doc 5 p. 10 calls the core-technology choice premature.

F1.quote: The Bank would receive payment messages instructing transfers on the core ledger in anonymised form and would not know the identity of the payer and payee.
F1.justification: The joint BoE–HMT proposal says the Bank receives payment messages in anonymised form and would not know payer or payee identity. This is a statement of inability to know, not only that the Bank will not use the data. PIPs anonymise personal data before any sharing with the Bank (doc 3 p. 16, p. 74). The consultation response turns this into a commitment backed by intended legislation (doc 4 p. 28). The 2026 update reports technical and structural safeguards in the architecture (doc 17 p. 7). No routine identity key held by the Bank is documented, so the value is no rather than yes.

F2.quote: The alias design allows privacy for the payer from the payee and vice versa, but not privacy from their PIPs.
F2.justification: The Bank's technical paper states explicitly that a user's own wallet provider knows who they are even when a disposable alias is used. The privacy design protects users from counterparties, not from their PIP. The joint CP gives PIPs the identity records and says personal data is anonymised only before sharing with the Bank, which implies PIP-side linkage (doc 3 p. 16, p. 57). The point-of-sale PoC shows transaction data viewable by payer and payee PIPs (doc 6 p. 22, tested). The value rests on an explicit statement, not on the KYC-plus-intermediation inference barred by §6.5.

F3.quote: any law enforcement or Government agency that seeks to access and process digital pound users’ personal data from PIPs would have to do so on a lawful basis in compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018.
F3.justification: The PIP is named as the holder from which authorities obtain personal data, so the route is via_PSP and not n/d. The consultation response confirms that law enforcement engages with PIPs 'and not directly with the Bank' (doc 4 p. 29). The 2020 paper adds suspicious-transaction reporting by PIPs (doc 1 p. 32). No route via the CB is documented.

F4.quote: Our current thinking is that this functionality would not be available at launch, but we will continue to explore device offline payments and review this position.
F4.justification: No offline mode is an adopted commitment. The design note proposes only deferred offline payments, in which funds remain on the ledger and settle once a party reconnects (doc 16 p. 4). Those payments therefore pass through the ordinary PIP-linked flow, so they are not private. Device offline, the only potentially private mode, is excluded at launch under current thinking. Experiments that tested device offline do not establish adoption (doc 12 p. 14: no final decision). Because the status is option, this is not a commitment.

F7.quote: Just like opening a bank or other payment account, some level of identity verification would be required when opening a digital pound wallet, in order to prevent financial crime.
F7.justification: Every wallet requires some level of identity verification, and the same wording is repeated in the response (doc 4 p. 28). The tiered wallets that are envisaged accept 'limited ID' (doc 3 p. 77). That is KYC-lite that still verifies identity, so it does not count as a no-identity route. The value is explicit; the §6.6a inference is not needed.

F8.quote: To establish and maintain these relationships, PIPs would require identity information of wallet account holders, which would allow them to carry out KYC checks and comply with AML regulations.
F8.justification: PIPs require identity information and run KYC checks for wallet holders. The response confirms that PIPs would be required to identify users (doc 4 p. 28). The design note on intermediaries lists KYC at onboarding among PIP duties (doc 14 p. 7).

F9.quote: In addition to law enforcement to fight crime (operating via law enforcement agencies engaging with PIPs under rules already approved by Parliament and not directly with the Bank), these are likely to be limited to:
F9.justification: The response names the extraordinary circumstances in which personal data held by PIPs becomes relevant to authorities. These are law enforcement, PIP failure and dispute resolution, governed by a data framework to be approved by Parliament (doc 4 p. 28). This prevents F1 = no from being read as absolute. The list beyond law enforcement is hedged as 'likely'.

F10.quote: Programmable money would be both prohibited through primary legislation and technically impossible in the architecture.
F10.justification: The authorities ruled out government- or central bank-initiated programmable functions (doc 3 p. 83) and committed to a legislative guarantee (doc 4 p. 31). Programmability is limited to PIP features that require user consent. Holding limits are a cap on balances, not purpose, expiry or blocking restrictions.

F12.quote: We are continuing our evaluations of various ledger technologies and architectures, including relational databases, NoSQL and distributed ledger technologies
F12.justification: The technical paper leans towards centrally governed distributed databases but keeps a range of approaches under assessment (doc 2 p. 52; doc 5 p. 18). The CP calls the platform model technology-agnostic (doc 3 p. 57). The 2025 update confirms evaluations of ledger technologies are ongoing. Lab and prototype-ledger work are tests, not choices (doc 17 p. 5; doc 18 p. 9).

F11.primary_objectives: cash_substitute_resilience + monetary_sovereignty_transmission (sustain access to central bank money / singleness); payment_modernisation + innovation_competitiveness (innovation, choice, efficiency)
